q: In the four-component view of a computer system, which ordering runs from bottom to top?
explain: Hardware sits at the bottom, the OS coordinates it, applications use resources to solve problems, and users (people, programs, or other computers) direct the work.

q: Who manages the CPU cache level of the storage hierarchy?
explain: Registers are managed by the compiler, cache by hardware, and main memory, SSDs, and magnetic disks by the operating system.

q: The kernel and the operating system are synonyms.
explain: The kernel is the always-running core. The full OS also includes system programs and, on modern systems, middleware.

q: A trap (exception) differs from a hardware interrupt because it is:
choices: Generated by software, from an error or a system call
explain: A trap is a software-generated interrupt caused by an error (divide by zero, page fault) or a user request such as a system call. It uses the same handling machinery.

q: Why does DMA improve performance for high-speed devices?
choices: It raises one interrupt per byte so data is never lost
It lets the device controller move whole blocks to memory with one interrupt per block
It turns the device into a volatile cache
It makes the CPU poll the device constantly
explain: With Direct Memory Access the controller transfers entire blocks between its buffer and main memory, generating one interrupt per block, so the CPU is free for other work.

q: A user program can switch the mode bit to kernel mode by itself whenever it needs a privileged instruction.
explain: The only legitimate route into kernel mode is a system call, trap, or interrupt, which the OS controls. The mode bit resets to user on return.

q: What guarantees the OS regains control from a process stuck in an infinite loop?
explain: The OS sets a timer through a privileged instruction before scheduling a process. When it counts down to zero it raises an interrupt, returning control to the OS.

q: Explain the difference between multiprogramming and multitasking (timesharing).
answer: Multiprogramming keeps several jobs in memory and switches to another job when the current one must wait (for example for I/O), so the CPU is never idle. Multitasking goes further: it switches among jobs rapidly on a timer so every user can interact with each job while it runs, producing interactive response.
explain: Key contrast: multiprogramming switches only when a job blocks; multitasking switches frequently to give responsiveness.

q: Which I/O subsystem technique overlaps the output of one job with the input of others, as in print queues?
explain: Spooling queues output (classically print jobs). Buffering holds data in transit; caching keeps copies in faster storage.

q: What is abstraction in an operating system? Give one concrete example.
answer: Abstraction hides device and architecture details behind simple, consistent interfaces so programmers do not deal with the hardware directly. Example: the OS exposes a file with open/read/write/close, so programs never deal with disk sectors, RPM, or controller commands.
explain: The notes flag this as a classic exam question: give the definition plus a concrete case.

q: Which parameter-passing method for system calls is used by Linux and places no limit on the number or length of parameters?
choices: A memory block whose address is passed in a register
explain: Linux stores parameters in a memory block/table and passes its address in a register. The block and stack methods don't limit parameter count or length.

q: Background services (daemons) run in kernel mode.
explain: Daemons are system programs launched at boot that run in user mode, not kernel mode.

q: In a program that calls fork() and then execl("/bin/ls", ...) in the child, what happens to a printf placed right after the successful execl?
choices: It never runs because the child's code was replaced by ls
explain: A successful exec overlays the calling process with the new executable, so there is no original code left to return to.

q: What is the difference between an API and an ABI?
choices: They are the same thing on POSIX systems
An API is source-level; an ABI is the binary-level interface for compiled code on a specific OS and CPU
An ABI is for Java only
An API defines calling conventions; an ABI defines function names
explain: The notes' exact phrasing: the ABI is the architecture equivalent of an API. API = how you write code; ABI = how compiled bytes interoperate.

q: Which OS structure moves as much functionality as possible into user space and communicates through message passing?
explain: A microkernel (Mach is the classic example) keeps the kernel tiny. It is more reliable and secure but pays message-passing overhead.

q: What does the loader do?
choices: Combines object files into one executable
Translates C source into object code
Brings an executable into memory and performs relocation
explain: The linker combines object files into an executable; the loader copies it into memory, assigning final addresses (relocation).

q: A plain (unbalanced) binary search tree has O(log n) search time.
explain: A general BST is O(n) because it can degenerate into a linked list. Only a balanced BST guarantees O(log n).

q: Distinguish protection from security as OS services.
answer: Protection ensures that all access to system resources is controlled, so concurrent processes cannot interfere with each other (an internal concern). Security defends the system from outsiders, which requires user authentication and guarding external I/O devices such as network adapters from invalid access.
explain: Protection is internal control of access; security is defense against external threats.

q: macOS's Darwin kernel is best described as:
choices: A hybrid combining the Mach microkernel with BSD UNIX parts
A layered kernel with no modules
A microkernel with no BSD components
explain: macOS is a hybrid, layered OS; Darwin combines Mach and BSD, with an I/O kit and loadable kernel extensions.

q: What does (int)3.99 evaluate to in C?
explain: Casting float to int truncates the fractional part; it does not round.

q: How many bytes is a long on a typical 64-bit system (versus 32-bit)?
explain: long grows from 4 bytes on 32-bit to 8 bytes on 64-bit, a classic portability bug.

q: Given int *p, *q; what does *q = *p do?
choices: Makes q point where p points
Copies the value p points to into the location q points to
explain: q = p is pointer assignment; *q = *p copies the pointed-to value.

q: You can compare two structs of the same type with ==.
explain: Structs can be assigned with = but not compared with == or !=; compare member by member.

q: After free(ptr); the pointer ptr still holds the old address. What is ptr called, and what is the fix?
choices: A memory leak; call free again
A dangling pointer; set ptr = NULL
A null pointer; nothing to fix
explain: free releases the block but does not change the pointer. Set it to NULL immediately after freeing.

q: Contrast a memory leak with a dangling pointer.
answer: A memory leak is memory that is still allocated but every pointer to it was lost, so it can never be freed. A dangling pointer is a pointer you still have to memory that was already freed, so it points at nothing valid. They are opposite mistakes.
explain: Leak: memory without a pointer. Dangling: pointer without memory.

q: Given printf("One\n"); fork(); printf("Two\n"); how many times does each line print?
explain: Code before the fork runs once; code after runs in both the parent and child.

q: What does fork() return in the child process?
explain: fork is called once but returns twice: 0 in the child, the child's PID in the parent, and -1 on failure.

q: How many processes exist after three consecutive fork() calls, counting the original?
explain: n forks create 2^n processes, so 2^3 = 8.

q: Which allocation function zero-clears the block it returns?
explain: calloc(n, size) allocates and zeroes; malloc does not initialize; realloc resizes.

q: When exec() replaces a process's code, its PID changes.
explain: Only the code being executed changes. The PID and PPID stay the same.

q: Which process memory section holds function parameters, return addresses, and local variables?
explain: Text holds code, data holds globals, the heap holds malloc'd memory, and the stack holds temporary call data.

q: A process finishes waiting for I/O. Which state does it move to next?
explain: A waiting process returns to Ready, not directly to Running; it still needs the scheduler to give it a CPU.

q: In Linux, the process control block is the C structure:
explain: Linux represents the PCB with task_struct.

q: Context-switch time is pure overhead; no useful work is done during it.
explain: The switch itself accomplishes nothing. Its cost grows with OS and PCB complexity and depends on hardware support.

q: Why is shared memory faster than message passing?
choices: After setup, access is ordinary memory reads and writes with no kernel involvement
explain: The kernel is only needed to set up the region. Message passing traps into the kernel on every send and receive.

q: In the bounded-buffer solution with in and out indices (no counter), the buffer is full when:
explain: Full is (in + 1) % SIZE == out and empty is in == out, which sacrifices one slot to tell them apart.

q: Why does adding a shared counter to the producer-consumer buffer create a race condition?
answer: counter++ and counter-- are not atomic. Each compiles to three steps: load into a register, add or subtract, store back. If the producer's and consumer's steps interleave, one update is lost, so counter can end up 4 or 6 instead of 5. The in/out version had no race because each process modified only its own variable.
explain: The race comes from both processes writing the same variable with unsynchronized read-modify-write sequences.

q: For an unnamed pipe created with int fd[2]; pipe(fd);, which end is which?
choices: It depends on which process calls fork first
explain: fd[0] is the read end and fd[1] is the write end. Unnamed pipes are one-way; two-way communication needs two pipes.

q: If both send and receive are blocking, the meeting point is called a:
explain: Blocking send plus blocking receive is a rendezvous, which is also what zero-capacity buffering forces.

q: On Android, which process type is killed first when memory runs low?
explain: Importance from most to least: foreground, visible, service, background, empty. Empty processes are reclaimed first.

q: Which of these does each thread have its own copy of?
explain: Each thread owns its TID, program counter, registers, and stack. Code, data, heap, and OS resources are shared.

q: Concurrency requires multiple CPU cores.
explain: Concurrency means multiple tasks make progress, which a single core does by interleaving them. Parallelism, where tasks run at the same instant, requires multiple cores.

q: A program is 25% serial. What is the speedup going from 1 to 2 cores according to Amdahl's Law?
A program is 10% serial. What is the maximum possible speedup with unlimited cores?
explain: As N grows without bound, speedup approaches 1/S = 1/0.10 = 10.

q: Compute the speedup for a program that is 90% parallel on 4 cores. Show the formula.
explain: Only the parallel portion is divided by N. The ceiling for this program is 10x.

q: In the many-to-one threading model, what happens when one thread makes a blocking system call?
choices: The kernel creates a new kernel thread
The thread is migrated to another core
explain: All user threads share one kernel thread, so a blocking call stalls every thread. Many-to-one also cannot run threads in parallel.

q: Linux and Windows use which threading model?
explain: Each user thread maps to its own kernel thread.

q: It is possible to create a thread library without any kernel-level support.
explain: A user-level library can implement creation, context switching, scheduling, and synchronization entirely in user space.

q: Why should a Pthread return a value through malloc'd memory rather than the address of a local variable?
choices: The thread's stack is gone once the thread exits, so the address would be invalid
pthread_exit only accepts heap pointers by type
Heap memory is automatically freed on join
explain: A local lives on the thread's private stack, which disappears at exit. Heap memory persists until freed.

q: Sending CTRL+C (an asynchronous signal) to a multithreaded process should generally be delivered to:
choices: Only the thread that caused it
explain: Synchronous signals go to the thread that caused them; asynchronous ones like CTRL+C are generally sent to all threads.

q: Which cancellation approach lets the target thread stop at a safe point?
explain: With deferred cancellation, the target periodically checks whether it should terminate. Asynchronous cancellation can leave shared data half-updated.

q: Summing a huge array by giving each core its own slice is an example of:
explain: Data parallelism runs the same operation on different chunks of data. Task parallelism runs different operations.

q: Under non-preemptive scheduling, scheduling decisions occur only when a process:
choices: Moves from running to ready, or from waiting to ready
Moves from running to waiting, or terminates
explain: Situations 1 (running → waiting) and 4 (terminate) force a decision. Situations 2 and 3 are the extra choices preemptive scheduling adds.

q: The time it takes the dispatcher to stop one process and start another is called:
explain: Dispatch latency is pure overhead paid on every switch.

q: Which scheduling criteria should be maximized?
explain: Maximize CPU utilization and throughput; minimize turnaround, waiting, and response time.

q: Processes P1 (burst 24), P2 (3), and P3 (3) arrive in order P1, P2, P3 under FCFS. Compute the average waiting time and average turnaround time.
answer: Gantt chart: P1 0–24, P2 24–27, P3 27–30. Waiting times are 0, 24, and 27, so the average is 51/3 = 17. Turnaround times are 24, 27, and 30, so the average is 81/3 = 27.
explain: If they arrive in order P2, P3, P1 instead, the average wait drops to 3, which shows the convoy effect.

q: Short processes stuck waiting behind one long CPU-bound process under FCFS is called:
explain: The convoy effect is FCFS's signature weakness and the motivation for SJF.

q: Using SJF, compute the average waiting time for P1 (6), P2 (8), P3 (7), P4 (3), all arriving at time 0.
explain: SJF is optimal: it gives the minimum average waiting time for a given set of processes.

q: With exponential averaging and α = 0.5, the previous prediction was 10 ms and the actual burst was 6 ms. What is the next prediction?
With α = 0 in exponential averaging, the prediction always equals the most recent actual burst.
explain: α = 0 ignores the recent burst, so the prediction never changes. α = 1 makes it equal the most recent burst.

q: The preemptive version of SJF is:
explain: SRTF preempts the running process if a newly arrived process has a shorter remaining burst.

q: What does SJF's "shortest job" actually compare?
explain: It compares the upcoming CPU burst, which is why predicting that burst is the practical challenge.

q: Which is NOT one of the three requirements for a critical-section solution?
explain: The three requirements are mutual exclusion, progress, and bounded waiting.

q: The simple turn-variable solution (while (turn == j);) fails which requirement?
explain: It forces strict alternation. If it is Pj's turn but Pj never wants to enter, Pi is locked out of an empty critical section.

q: Write the entry section of Peterson's solution for process Pi, and explain in one sentence why it provides mutual exclusion.
answer: flag[i] = true; turn = j; while (flag[j] && turn == j); Mutual exclusion holds because Pi enters only if flag[j] is false or turn == i, and turn is a single variable that cannot equal both i and j, so both processes cannot pass at once.
explain: Exit section: flag[i] = false. On modern CPUs, Peterson's needs memory barriers because independent writes can be reordered.

q: Why can Peterson's solution fail on modern architectures?
choices: Processors and compilers may reorder independent writes, and memory may be weakly ordered
It only works with more than two processes
explain: Reordering the writes to flag[i] and turn can let both processes into their critical sections. Memory barriers force visibility.

q: A lock built from test_and_set() with a busy-wait loop satisfies which requirements?
choices: Mutual exclusion and progress, but not bounded waiting
explain: An unlucky process can lose the TAS race forever. Adding the waiting[] array with a circular scan restores bounded waiting.

q: compare_and_swap(&lock, 0, 1) returns:
explain: CAS atomically returns the original value and swaps only if *value equals expected.

q: A semaphore whose value is -3 under the blocking-queue implementation means:
choices: Three processes are blocked waiting on it
explain: In the no-busy-wait version, a negative value's magnitude equals the number of waiting processes.

q: To force P1's statement S1 to run before P2's S2, initialize semaphore sync to:
explain: P1: S1; signal(sync). P2: wait(sync); S2. Starting at 0 means the event has not happened yet, so P2 blocks until P1 signals.

q: A process calls wait(mutex) twice in a row without a signal in between. What happens?
choices: The process blocks permanently on the second wait
The semaphore becomes a counting semaphore
explain: Double wait deadlocks the process and makes the semaphore unavailable to everyone. Reversing the order (signal then wait) violates mutual exclusion.

q: A condition variable's x.signal() with no waiting process is remembered, just like a semaphore signal().
explain: x.signal() with no waiters has no effect. A semaphore signal() always increments the value.

q: Distinguish deadlock from livelock.
answer: In deadlock, processes are blocked waiting on each other and do nothing. In livelock, processes are actively running, constantly reacting and yielding to each other, but still make no progress, like two people stepping aside the same way in a hallway.
explain: Both mean zero progress. Deadlock is idle; livelock burns CPU.

q: Why does disabling interrupts fail as a general critical-section solution?
choices: It is too slow on one CPU
It does not stop another core from entering the critical section, and long sections can starve others
It violates mutual exclusion on a uniprocessor
explain: It is not scalable to multiprocessors and can starve processes if the section runs long.

q: In the bounded-buffer semaphore solution, what are the initial values of mutex, empty, and full for a buffer of size n?
explain: The buffer is free (mutex = 1), all n slots are empty (empty = n), and none are full (full = 0).

q: What happens if the producer swaps its two waits to wait(mutex); wait(empty); and the buffer is full?
answer: Deadlock. The producer takes the mutex, then blocks on empty because no slots are free. The consumer passes wait(full) but blocks on wait(mutex), which the sleeping producer holds. Each waits for something only the other can provide. Rule: acquire the counting semaphore first and the mutex last.
explain: Swapping the two signals only hurts efficiency; swapping the two waits kills the program.

q: In the reader-priority readers-writers solution, which reader releases rw_mutex?
choices: The last reader to leave (when read_count hits 0)
explain: Only the first reader locks rw_mutex and only the last one out unlocks it. Readers in between just update read_count.

q: In the readers-writers solution, what does the inner mutex protect?
explain: read_count++ and read_count-- are not atomic, so mutex prevents lost updates that would make the first/last-reader tests fire at the wrong time.

q: The reader-priority readers-writers solution can starve writers.
explain: A continuous stream of overlapping readers keeps read_count above 0, so signal(rw_mutex) never runs.

q: The naive dining philosophers solution (one semaphore per chopstick, grab left then right) can:
choices: Deadlock if all five grab their left chopstick at once
explain: Every chopstick is held and every philosopher waits on a neighbor, which is a circular wait.

q: The monitor solution to dining philosophers eliminates both deadlock and starvation.
explain: It eliminates deadlock by granting both chopsticks atomically, but a philosopher can still starve while both neighbors alternate eating.

q: In POSIX, the equivalents of semaphore wait() and signal() are:
explain: There is no sem_signal. signal() maps to sem_post().

q: Which POSIX semaphore type can be shared by unrelated processes?
explain: Named semaphores have a string name that unrelated processes can open. Unnamed ones are shared only through fork or shared memory.

q: Why must pthread_cond_wait be called inside a while loop rather than an if?
answer: Between the moment a waiter is signaled and the moment it reacquires the mutex, another thread may have changed the condition again, or the wait may return spuriously. The while loop rechecks the condition on every wakeup; an if would proceed on a stale condition.
explain: The same rule applies to Java's wait() inside synchronized methods.

q: In Java, a thread that called wait() inside a synchronized method is placed in the object's:
explain: The entry set holds threads waiting to acquire the lock. The wait set holds threads that gave up the lock by calling wait(). notify() moves one from the wait set to the entry set.

q: On a single-CPU Linux system, spinlock acquire and release are replaced by:
explain: Spinning makes no sense with no other CPU to release the lock.

q: List and define the four necessary conditions for deadlock.
answer: 1) Mutual exclusion: at least one resource is held in a non-sharable mode. 2) Hold and wait: a process holds at least one resource while waiting for others. 3) No preemption: resources cannot be forcibly taken away; only the holder can release them. 4) Circular wait: a cycle of processes exists where each waits for a resource held by the next.
explain: All four must hold at once. Breaking any one makes deadlock impossible.

q: A resource-allocation graph contains a cycle, and every resource type has a single instance. What can you conclude?
explain: No cycle → no deadlock. Cycle with single instances → deadlock. Cycle with multiple instances → maybe; run graph reduction.

q: A cycle in a resource-allocation graph with multi-instance resources always means deadlock.
explain: A process outside the cycle may hold an instance it will release, breaking the cycle.

q: Deadlock, livelock, and starvation differ as follows. Which statement is correct?
choices: All deadlocked processes are starved, but starved processes are usually not deadlocked
explain: Deadlock is blocked forever in a cycle; livelock is running but making no progress; starvation is one process indefinitely postponed while the system progresses.

q: In an expedient system, a knot in the resource graph is:
choices: Necessary but not sufficient for deadlock
explain: Expedient + knot ⟹ deadlock. A cycle is necessary; a knot is not necessary in general.

q: When consumable resources are involved, the order of graph reduction can change the verdict.
explain: With consumable resources reducibility may be order-dependent, and complete reducibility is no longer equivalent to freedom from deadlock.

q: In the Banker's Algorithm, Need is computed as:
explain: Need[i][j] is the remaining claim: the maximum claim minus what is currently allocated.

q: An unsafe state is the same as a deadlocked state.
explain: Unsafe means deadlock is possible in some worst-case future. The Banker's Algorithm avoids unsafe states so luck is never required.

q: Which deadlock prevention approach is the practical winner?
choices: Impose a total ordering and request resources in ascending order
explain: Resource ordering makes circular wait impossible; the other approaches are infeasible or wasteful.

q: Contrast deadlock prevention with deadlock avoidance.
answer: Prevention breaks one of the four necessary conditions by design, so it needs no runtime information or per-request check, but it is restrictive and can waste resources. Avoidance allows all four conditions but uses runtime information, the declared maximum claim, to refuse requests that would lead to an unsafe state, running a check such as the Banker's Algorithm on every request. It is more flexible but has runtime overhead and requires maxima to be declared up front.
explain: Detection and recovery is the third option: allow deadlock, find it, and pay the recovery cost.

q: Why is killing and restarting a deadlocked process not free?
choices: Process execution is generally not idempotent, so restarting can repeat side effects
It always causes a new deadlock
explain: A process that already printed or sent messages cannot simply be re-run without repeating those effects.

q: Two processes each request 40 blocks, then another 40 (P1), or 30 then 50 (P2), from 100 blocks. After both first requests are granted, what happens?
choices: Deadlock: 30 blocks are free but P1 needs 40 and P2 needs 50
explain: 70 of 100 are allocated. Neither remaining request can be satisfied, so they deadlock on quantities of a single resource type.

q: The base register is 300040 and the limit register is 120900. What is the highest legal address?
explain: Legal addresses satisfy base ≤ address < base + limit, so the highest is 300040 + 120900 − 1 = 420939.

q: Absolute code can be generated for which binding time?
explain: Only when the memory location is known at compile time can addresses be hard-coded.

q: The mapping of logical to physical addresses is done in hardware by the:
explain: The MMU performs run-time mapping; the relocation register is a component it uses.

q: Which placement strategy produces the smallest leftover hole?
explain: Best-fit picks the smallest hole that fits. Worst-fit leaves the largest leftover. First-fit and best-fit beat worst-fit in speed and utilization.

q: Compaction is possible only if relocation is dynamic and done at execution time.
explain: Moving a process mid-run requires translating addresses through a register the OS can update.

q: Paging eliminates which kind of fragmentation?
explain: Any page fits any frame, so there is no external fragmentation. Internal fragmentation remains in each process's last page.

q: With 4-byte pages and a page table mapping page 0→5, 1→6, 2→1, 3→2, translate logical address 13 to a physical address.
answer: page = 13 ÷ 4 = 3, offset = 13 mod 4 = 1. Page 3 maps to frame 2. Physical address = 2 × 4 + 1 = 9.
explain: General recipe: p = floor(addr / pagesize), d = addr mod pagesize, physical = frame(p) × pagesize + d.

q: Page size is 2,048 bytes and a process is 72,766 bytes. How many frames does it need, and how much internal fragmentation is there?
answer: 72,766 ÷ 2,048 = 35 full pages with 1,086 bytes left over, so it needs 36 frames. Internal fragmentation = 2,048 − 1,086 = 962 bytes.
explain: Worst case wastes one frame minus one byte; the average is half a frame per process.

q: With a 10 ns memory access, a TLB hit ratio of 80%, and free TLB lookup, what is the effective access time?
explain: EAT = 0.80 × 10 + 0.20 × 20 = 12 ns, a 20% slowdown. At a 99% hit ratio it is 10.1 ns.

q: Without ASID support in the TLB, what must happen on each context switch?
explain: Otherwise the next process would use the previous process's translations.

q: A 32-bit logical address space with 4 KB pages and 4-byte entries needs how much memory for one flat page table?
explain: 2^32 / 2^12 = 2^20 entries × 4 bytes = 4 MB per process, which is why the page table itself gets paged.

q: Dynamic loading requires special operating system support.
explain: Dynamic loading is implemented through program design. Dynamic linking (stubs and shared libraries) is the OS-supported mechanism.

q: With a 1 KB page size, what are the page number and offset for address 3085?
A system has a 32-bit logical address, 4 KB pages, and 512 MB of physical memory. How many entries are in a conventional page table and in an inverted page table?
answer: Conventional: 2^32 / 2^12 = 2^20 = 1,048,576 entries per process. Inverted: 512 MB / 4 KB = 2^29 / 2^12 = 2^17 = 131,072 entries for the whole system.
explain: A conventional table is sized by logical space per process; an inverted table is sized by physical memory for the whole system.

q: What is a known drawback of inverted page tables?
choices: They use more memory than conventional tables
Lookups require searching, and shared memory is awkward
They cannot be used with a TLB
explain: Each frame records one mapping, and lookups search for (pid, page), mitigated by hashing and the TLB.

q: Each element in a hashed page table's chain contains:
choices: Virtual page number, mapped frame, and a pointer to the next element
The outer and inner page indices
explain: Translation walks the chain comparing virtual page numbers until one matches.

q: A 100 MB process is swapped out to a hard drive at 140 MB/s and a same-size process is swapped in. Estimate the context-switch time.
answer: Swap out: 100 / 140 ≈ 714 ms. Swap in: another ≈ 714 ms. Total ≈ 1,428 ms, about 1.4 seconds.
explain: On an NVMe SSD at 14,700 MB/s, the total is about 13.6 ms, still huge next to a normal context switch.

q: iOS and Android support paging but typically do not support swapping.
explain: Flash has limited write cycles, small capacity, and poor throughput on mobile. iOS asks apps to free memory; Android terminates apps after saving state.

q: How is the IA-32 16-bit segment selector divided?
explain: s = 13 bits, g = 1 bit (GDT vs LDT), p = 2 bits.

q: For 4 KB pages, IA-32 splits the 32-bit linear address as:
explain: 10 bits index the page directory, 10 bits index the page table, and 12 bits are the offset. A 4 MB page uses a 22-bit offset.

q: PAE on IA-32 allows up to how much physical memory?
explain: PAE uses three-level paging with 64-bit entries for 36-bit physical addresses (64 GB). Virtual addresses stay 32-bit.

q: x86-64 in practice implements:
choices: 48-bit virtual and 52-bit physical addresses with four-level paging
explain: Page sizes are 4 KB, 2 MB, or 1 GB.

q: On an ARM memory reference, which TLB is checked first?
explain: The micro TLB is checked first, then the main TLB, then the CPU walks the page table itself.

q: Swapping and paging solve the same problem.
explain: Paging is an address-translation scheme that removes contiguity. Swapping is a capacity scheme that moves memory to disk. You can page without swapping.
